summary:
Danig turns NASA Earth Information Center visualizations into sound. Most NASA data is shown through colour: bright maps, gradients and animations. That leaves out people who are blind or have low vision, and it can mislead people who are colour-blind or have blurry vision, because the meaning is carried by colour they can’t reliably tell apart. Our web app reads each video frame, matches every pixel to the colour legend to recover the real data value, and turns that value into music: low values sound low, high values sound high. 

Users can also upload any map video and its colour legend, and the engine sonifies it automatically. It matters because climate science should be understandable by everyone, not only people who can see a colour bar.
details:
DANIG Details

Website Link
https://nasa-blackbellch-jukebox.vercel.app/


What it does and how it works

  • It is a playlist of preset NASA datasets: rain (IMERG), near-surface temperature, carbon monoxide, ozone and nitrogen oxides.
  • Users can upload their own video and a picture of its colour legend, and it is sonified the same way.
  • The engine reads the legend image to build a table of colour-to-value pairs. Each video frame is analysed in the browser, and every pixel is matched to the nearest legend colour to recover its true value. Colours that aren’t on the legend, such as borders, labels and no-data areas, stay silent.
  • The listener picks a place by clicking the map or using the arrow keys. Every 250 ms the value at that spot becomes a note: a lower value is a lower pitch, a higher value is a higher pitch, and a stronger value is louder.
  • Sound in the left ear is west and sound in the right ear is east. A quiet low drone follows the average of the whole planet.
  • When a place is warmer or wetter than its own early baseline, a second, slightly clashing note joins in, so change can be heard, not only the current value.

Benefits and intended impact

  • It makes NASA’s visual data usable without sight, and without telling colours apart.
  • It lets blind and low-vision users explore data independently, not through someone else’s description.
  • It gives everyone else a second sense for reading patterns. Sound can reveal changes over time that are easy to miss by eye.
  • It also builds an emotional connection to the planet: a rainforest sounds like rain, and a heat wave sounds like heat.

Making the sound pleasant

  • A single tone mapped straight from data is repetitive and tiring to hear for long.
  • We put every note on a pentatonic scale, major or minor, so any value sounds in key and nothing clashes.
  • We layered a nature-style texture under the notes. Users can switch the scene layer to suit their taste.
  • Users can also switch instruments and scales.

Creative choices

  • Each instrument is built from raw Web Audio oscillators and filters, with no audio samples:
    • Piano: every note is a rolled chord. Higher values give a bright major third and lower values a darker minor third, so the chord carries a second reading of the data.
    • Xylophone: three partials tuned at 1:3:6 give the hollow wooden “tok”, and short notes keep fast data readable.
    • Accordion: two reeds detuned either side of the pitch give the shimmer, with a nasal filter peak and a slow bellows swell.
    • Harp: detuned strings that darken as they fade, plus a ghost echo an octave up.
    • Flute: a sine tone with vibrato and a breath-noise layer.
    • Sparkle: a glass celesta whose small grace notes follow the current scale.
    • Bell, ice chime and water drip: inharmonic bell partials for the bell and ice chime, and a drip that falls onto its pitch.
    • Pluck: a plucked-string tone.
  • The scene layers are also built from oscillators and filtered noise. Rain is drips and a wash. Heat is a buzzing pad with glassy chimes. The sea is a slow swell, snow is a hush, and a city hums. Air is thin and glassy, and extreme rain adds distant thunder.

Accessibility

  • The whole app works by keyboard.
  • A screen reader announces every action, place name and value.
  • A Sound key (K) plays eight notes from the lowest to the highest value as a short listening lesson. It pauses playback so nothing talks over it.
  • The Describe key (D) reads out what is happening now.
  • On-screen text is kept to what matters, with four text sizes (T) and a fixed-size Settings box.
  • Reduced-motion settings are respected.

Tools

  • HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript, with no frameworks.
  • The Web Audio API for synthesis, filters and reverb.
  • The Canvas API for reading video pixels.
  • A small Python server with a proxy for loading remote video.
  • NASA EIC videos and colour legends as input. No machine learning is used.
  • It runs in any modern browser, with no special hardware.

Factors we considered

  • Musicality against faithful data, so the sound is neither noise nor decoration.
  • Listening fatigue.
  • Colour-blindness and low vision, since the app matches colours to a legend and the user never has to tell them apart.
  • Keyboard-only and screen-reader use.
  • Large text on small screens.
  • Honest silence when there is no data.
dataRefs: Near Real-Time Global Precipitation from the Global Precipitation Measurement Constellation
